In a landscape dominated by hype and fear, clear, reliable and nuanced information about the true capabilities of AI remains strikingly absent. Even AI developers do not understand the current capacities of AI systems – or how rapidly they are advancing. As an independent and authoritative international body, the OECD is well positioned to fill this knowledge gap. Drawing on its experience in comparative assessment, extensive collaboration with leading computer scientists and engineers, and its international perspective, the OECD has developed a unique methodology to deliver rigorous, evidence-based and clear insights into the real-world performance of AI. This framework is known as the OECD AI Capability Indicators. It offers policy makers the clarity they urgently need to navigate an increasingly complex technological environment and craft informed, future-proof strategies. Following the introduction, this technical report comprises three chapters written by the AI and Future of Skills project, describing the development and limitations of the current scales. The proceeding nine chapters are technical reports for each of nine beta indicators: language; social interaction; problem solving; creativity; knowledge, learning and memory; metacognition and critical thinking; vision; manipulation; and robotic intelligence. In Chapter 13, possible methods for leveraging the indicators for analyses of tasks and occupations are also considered. The final chapter introduces a tenth indicator, consciousness, which was also developed but not released as a beta indicator as the ethical and social questions of consciousness in AI remain controversial. It is not yet clear whether the indicator will be reworked or completely excluded going forward. In the meantime, the OECD shares lessons learnt from the experience, as well as key comments from the reviewers, to further the discussion and develop the necessary consensus. The ten indicators featured in this volume cover a range of human abilities that each describe the development of AI towards full human equivalence. The indicators are presented as five-level scales, where the most challenging capabilities for AI systems are found towards the top. Each level includes a short description of the sorts of capabilities that AI systems at that level can perform accurately and consistently. The rating of current AI performance on each scale is linked to available evidence. The indicators are being published in beta form with an invitation for two critical groups of stakeholders to provide feedback: computer scientists, whose AI evaluation work provides the evidence for the indicators, and policy makers, whose ability to interpret and leverage the insights from the scales is critical for the development of informed decisions. The OECD will release the first full version of the indicators after feedback from stakeholders and the development of a systematic updating protocol. The indicators were developed over five years, drawing on a large network on AI researchers, psychologists and other experts. The chapters of this technical report were written by 32 experts and reviewed by another 25 experts. A shorter and more accessible overview of the indicators, which comprises a brief overview of the methodological approach to their development, has been published separately.
10  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Abel Baret, OECD Sam Mitchell, OECD Stuart Elliott, OECD The arrival of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI) systems in recent years highlights the need for new tools to monitor their rapid development. This opening chapter introduces the rationale for a new framework to help policy makers and researchers understand the true extent of AI capabilities and how they compare to human abilities. The chapter discusses how the indicators can be used to support analyses related to larger ethical and safety issues related to AI use; evaluation of the impact of AI on the workforce and the economy; and the impact of AI on education. After outlining the subsequent 13 chapters, it invites collaboration with the computer science and human psychology communities to strengthen the indicators into a precise and responsive policy tool that can capture the critical implications of future AI developments. 1 Introduction  11 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Introduction Depending on the source, artificial intelligence (AI)1 is either set to save the world or destroy it. In a landscape dominated by hype and fear, clear, reliable and nuanced information about the true capabilities of AI remains strikingly absent. Even AI developers do not understand the current capacities of AI systems. With the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, AI and robotics are rapidly advancing, and policy makers worldwide recognise the need to assess their capability. In 2024, the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine revisited its 2017 review of Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work. It observed that policy makers still lack the information about AI capabilities that is needed to guide policy. Meanwhile, the AI Act of the European Union has called for its newly created AI Office to regularly monitor AI capabilities (EUR-Lex, 2024[1]). For their part, the OECD Council’s AI Recommendation and the Statement of the 2025 Paris AI Summit (OECD Legal Instruments, 2024[2]; La Maison Élysée, 2025[3]) emphasise the importance of understanding AI’s influence on the job market. Internationally, policy makers have already acknowledged the importance of a clear understanding of AI capabilities for their work. However, without an evidence-based framework describing what AI can do, it will be impossible to respond appropriately to either questions of AI ethics and safety, or its impact on education or jobs. While technical initiatives (MLCommons, 2025[4]; PAI, n.d.[5]) seek to quantify the computing efficiency of models, no equivalent effort has analysed what these models can and cannot do. As an independent and authoritative international body, the OECD is well positioned to fill this knowledge gap. Drawing on its experience of comparative assessment, extensive collaboration with leading computer scientists and engineers, and its international perspective, the OECD has developed a unique methodology to deliver rigorous, evidence-based and clear insights into the real-world performance of AI. This framework, developed within the AI and Future Skills project, is known as the AI Capability Indicators. It offers policy makers and researchers the clarity they urgently need to understand the true extent of AI capabilities and how they compare to human abilities.2 The initial result of this framework, the OECD’s beta AI Capability Indicators are presented here. OECD (2023[6]) identified four criteria for effective indicators of AI capabilities: 1. Understandable: They should be easy to interpret. They should communicate current strengths and limitations of AI in a straightforward manner and should be understandable to non-experts. This implies, among other things, there should only be a few of them. 2. Policy relevant: They should enable policy makers to draw conclusions about AI’s impact on education, employment and the economy. 3. Comprehensive: They should cover all key aspects of AI capabilities needed to understand their implications. 4. Responsive: They should indicate important developments in AI, which means they will have to be systematically updated at regular intervals. Linking AI capabilities to human abilities allows policy makers to gauge AI’s potential role in education, work and everyday life. Existing frameworks that characterise AI capabilities such as MLCommons (MLCommons, 2025[4]) and Stanford’s AI Index (Maslej et al., 2025[5]) discuss capabilities purely in terms of benchmark performance without any comparison to human abilities. Taken in isolation, benchmark results are unclear to non-AI experts, and even to AI researchers it is unclear how results relate to AI systems’ capacity to perform tasks in real-world situations. In a discussion of the limitations of current AI benchmarks, the authors of the 2025 AI Index report noted that “(t)o truly assess the capabilities of AI systems, more rigorous and comprehensive evaluations are needed” (Maslej et al., 2025[7]) The OECD’s framework is unique in its effort to compare AI capabilities to the full range of human abilities used in the job market, recognising that in many cases adequate AI 12  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 benchmarks for the advanced levels are still lacking. The indicators provide a conceptual framework for identifying or developing tests that can evaluate AI’s capabilities systematically across the full range of human skill domains relevant to life and employment. Frameworks based in AI performance on benchmarks without a human baseline risk being quickly overtaken by rapid AI developments. An additional benefit of grounding a framework to evaluate AI capabilities in human abilities is they are relatively fixed over time. In other words, the framework will remain stable and informative amid rapid AI progress until it truly surpasses the full range of human performance. Anthropic’s AI Economic Index (Handa et al., 2025[8]) adopted a novel approach to analysing the impact of AI developments on the economy by linking Claude.ai’s capabilities to some human tasks. This was performed by analysing millions of interactions between Claude large language models (LLMs) and users where tasks that could be linked to those found on the O*NET (a United States–based database that systematically describes the skills, tasks, and requirements of different occupations) were performed. However, this approach was limited to analyses of chat-based interactions with LLMs. As such, it did not aim to compare AI performance to the full range of human abilities used in occupations. To make our indicators understandable and relevant for policy makers, AI capabilities are linked to the human abilities familiar to the policy community. This approach achieves comprehensiveness by covering a wide range of AI and robotic systems, inclusive of but not limited to large language models (LLMs) and other forms of generative AI. The capabilities of these systems are also compared to the full range of human abilities. The OECD is committed to developing a feasible way to update the indicators at regular intervals to reflect significant developments in the state of the art. A request for help from the expert community Given the beta form of the indicators, the OECD needs continued collaboration with the computer scientists and policy makers. The indicators need to be strengthened to become a precise and responsive policy tool that can capture the critical implications of future AI developments. The beta status of the scales is thus a direct request to the expert community: If you think something is wrong with the current version of the scales, tell us how they need to be fixed. Example use cases The OECD is developing the AI Capability Indicators as a foundation for a range of policy analyses related to the implications of AI. Before introducing the scales and how they were developed in more detail, the report discusses how the indicators can be used to support analyses related to 1) larger ethical and safety issues related to AI use; 2) evaluation of the impact of AI on the workforce and the economy; and 3) the impact of AI on education. Proposals for how to develop the last two type of analyses using the indicators are outlined in Chapter 13. Using the indicators to analyse AI’s implications for jobs and the economy The indicators offer a framework to evaluate how AI affects our economies. One approach to the impact of AI on the labour market is to map AI capabilities to the tasks humans perform at work, which can provide insights into potential shifts in job roles. This provides the starting point for analyses related to AI’s implications for jobs and the economy, especially those occupations at risk of substantial levels of automation. This research could be analysed in a variety of ways to derive estimates for individual occupations, which could then be aggregated to support analyses for the overall economy.  13 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Chapter 13 describes the way the indicators can be linked to the ability demands of different occupations and tasks and proposes a methodology for constructing an AI Catch-up Index for a fine-grained analyses of job transformation as a result of AI. As the indicators are updated in future, the potential implications for specific occupations and the overall economy can then be directly in line with the latest ratings. With the link from the AI Capability Indicators to the implications for different occupations, policy makers could analyse the potential sensitivity of the results to changes in specific AI capabilities. This will make it possible to identify AI capabilities that should be tracked closely given their larger implications for employment. Of course, even if it is technologically possible to partially automate different occupations, AI may not necessarily be used to displace workers. Specific practical barriers to AI application may only be apparent from a more detailed analysis. Alternatively, the potential use of AI may be more expensive than people continuing to perform the function. This might be the case if the automatable task represents only a small part of an overall occupation and the resulting benefits are small. There might also be ethical or safety concerns with substituting AI for humans in particular types of tasks. The indicators do not address potential barriers to using AI. Rather, they provide a signal that AI could carry out substantial portions of occupations or tasks. This, in turn, invites an examination of whether other factors are likely to encourage or discourage the use of those capabilities. The AI Capability Indicators could also be used as a framework for monitoring the diffusion and application of AI. This would reveal whether the diffusion process changes as AI capabilities increase and begin to approach full human equivalence in different areas. Using the indicators to analyse AI’s implications for education The AI Capability Indicators can also be used to support policy conversations related to education. The indicators can help inform two primary sets of policy questions: 1) the use of AI to carry out instructional and administrative activities; and 2) appropriate learning goals for students. These two questions have different facets. The AI Capability Indicators, for example, can be used to consider how AI capabilities relate to the ability demands for teachers. How will AI affect the range of tasks currently undertaken by teachers? Questions related to AI’s implications for the appropriate learning goals for students also relates in part to the occupational analyses in the previous section. In broad strokes, large-scale shifts in the workforce are expected with potential transformations in the human role in carrying out tasks. These provide a picture of how abilities needed by adults are likely to evolve with greater AI capabilities. Although the picture is described in terms of the workplace, many tasks appear both inside and outside of work. This transformation poses challenges to the education sector in considering how to prepare students for their adult lives. What skills will students need as AI acquires more complex human capabilities. Should students continue to learn skills that AI already has? Are there skills that should be preserved for their intrinsic human value, regardless of their practical relevance? Which skills are prerequisites for higher-level capabilities that AI still lacks? What new skills will be essential for working and living effectively with powerful AI systems? Ethical and safety issues Ethical and safety concerns around AI are at the heart of public, media and policy debates. In response to the current generation of deep learning models, issues such as algorithmic discrimination, mass data exploitation and lack of transparency in AI decision making have fueled calls for stronger oversight, ethical safeguards and responsible regulation. 14  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Beyond concerns about the impact of training huge models on the environment and energy infrastructure, most ethical and safety issues related to AI revolve around their capabilities. Scenarios about job automation, for example, often point out that an AI system could make an objectively worse decision than a human. Perhaps it would neglect key factors that a human would consider or be unable to explain a result. In other cases, society may want a person to bear the moral responsibility for a decision – such as deciding to kill an opponent during a war. Society may also believe it is ethically important for a person to carry out a particular task, such as a doctor informing a patient about a fatal illness. Understanding the relevant AI capabilities will be important to appreciating the related ethical and safety issues, including how these concerns may shift as AI capabilities change. The current stage of development of LLMs, for example, has raised great concerns about AI’s hallucinations. Consequently, policymakers should understand the necessity of developing accurate factual recall and human-like critical thinking capabilities to protect us from being misled by AI systems. A quantifiable roadmap to AGI Beyond signaling the risks and opportunities posed by current AI systems, the AI Capability Indicators will also allow policymakers and the public to track AI developments in a systematic and evidenced based way. This will be particularly important as AI systems develop advanced capabilities at or beyond the human level. Tech leaders and commentators have discussed the potential for artificial general intelligence (AGI) and societal risks associated with “singularity” – the moment when AI systems surpass human intelligence across all domains and could potentially result in explosively fast change. When it reaches singularity, could AGI potentially prioritise self-preservation over human interests? Leaders from organisations have divergent opinions on the risks of AGI. Executives at OpenAI (Kelly, 2023[9]) and X (Acres, 2023[10]) have discussed the imminent risk to humanity of AGI. Others at Meta (Collins, 2025[11]), Anthropic (AI Today, 2025[12]) and Google (Dragan et al., 2 April 2025[13]), reference the imminent arrival of AGI without detailing its implications. In 2023, leading researchers and tech CEOs signed an open letter warning that AGI could pose an existential threat to humanity. Should policy makers take these concerns seriously? If not now, then when? The OECD scales provide a timely framework for policy makers to understand the proximity of current systems to AGI and the closer term risks posed by intermediate steps. The scales provide a clear way to characterise an AGI system in human terms: performance at the top of the scale (level 5) indicates full human equivalence. An AI system performing at level 5 could reproduce the full range of human abilities, including all key human aspects of those abilities. Outline of the report The remaining chapters present the beta scales, their development and their potential to be a valuable tool for policy makers to understand AI developments. Chapter 2 by Sam Mitchell, Stuart Elliott and Abel Baret outlines the OECD’s methodology for assessing AI capabilities across human-like skill domains rather than focusing on tasks. It surveys two major information sources – expert opinion and direct AI performance measures – highlighting each one’s strengths and limits. The chapter emphasises that human abilities form a finite set of essential capabilities, which AI is progressively acquiring. It concludes with details on the project’s iterative development process and next steps for refining the indicators. Chapter 3 by Sam Mitchell, Stuart Elliott and Abel Baret discusses the beta AI Capability Indicators’ current shortcomings and outlines steps for their refinement. The chapter highlights potential additions or  15 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 reorganisations of the scales, clarifies their boundaries and overlap, and emphasises the need to systematically track rapid AI developments. It proposes an ongoing, evidence-based update process, anchored by expert judgement and performance measures. This would be supplemented by a repository for new benchmarks and standards, ensuring the indicators evolve with AI’s progress. Chapter 4 by Yvette Graham, Arthur Graesser and Swen Riberio explore questions around language as one of the OECD Capability Indicators for AI. They consider how many dimensions of difficulty are needed to develop such a scale, reflecting on whether it should focus on the case of communication induced by language or on other aspects, such as reasoning. It also looks at whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems should be defined on a discrete or continuous cale. Finally, it asks whether the main challenge is integration of different language capabilities or improving performance of capabilities like reasoning. After examining the stakes and challenges, it proposes a six-dimensional scale to track advances of NLP and AI. Chapter 5 by António M. Fernandes, Ana Teresa Antunes, Rebecca Ramnauth, Nicholas C. Georgiou, Miguel Faria, Haohua Dong, Regina de Brito Duarte, Joana Brito, Henrique Correia da Fonseca, Ana Vilaça Carrasco, Inês Lobo, Rui Prada, Ana Paiva and Brian Scassellati presents a framework for evaluating the social intelligence of AI agents, structured across five levels and seven social components. Drawing from psychology and human-computer interaction, the chapter identifies core social skills – such as memory, identity and embodiment – and shows how they influence other capabilities. The model helps assess agents like ChatGPT and AIBO, and highlights ethical concerns around trust, influence and inequality linked to socially intelligent agents. Chapter 6 by Kenneth Forbus and Patrick Kyllonen introduces four dimensions for characterising AI problem solving. It presents a five-level scale ranging from domain-specific capabilities to systems with holistic professional expertise. The text emphasises the roles of solution properties, alternatives considered, professional knowledge and model formulation/interpretation. Illustrative benchmarks and examples underscore how current AI excels at well-formalised tasks but struggles with open-ended, socially grounded domains. The chapter concludes by highlighting future research avenues for bridging tacit knowledge and robust reasoning. Chapter 7 by Giorgio Franceschelli and Mirco Musolesi introduces a five-level scale for evaluating AI creativity, built upon four criteria from human creativity research – product, process, press and person. The chapter illustrates how current AI systems often exhibit novelty and value but lack autonomy and intention. It further discusses emerging ethical challenges, the scarcity of comprehensive benchmarks for creative outputs and the societal implications of future AI systems capable of human-like creative agency. Chapter 8 by Christian Lebiere introduces a structured scale for assessing knowledge, learning and memory capabilities in AI systems. By delineating five progressive dimensions – ranging from information retrieval to integrated knowledge – the scale provides a conceptual framework to track and evaluate AI’s cognitive advancements. It also highlights key trade-offs such as accuracy, efficiency and generalisation capacity. Additionally, the chapter introduces a set of measures to evaluate AI models at each level of the scale systematically, comprising computation cost, predictive accuracy, generalisation robustness and incremental learning capabilities. Finally, it touches on ethical considerations related to intellectual property, privacy, bias and manipulation that emerging AI paradigms should address. Chapter 9 by José Hernández-Orallo and Kexin-Jian Chen explore how metacognition and critical thinking have become increasingly relevant with the rise of agentic systems in AI, while remaining difficult to evaluate. The authors developed a scale to present as many domains of human cognition as possible for this study. They propose a five-level scale merging three dimensions: the need for critical thinking processes, the difficulty of calibrating knowns and unknowns, and the difficulty of identifying relevant information. Unlike other capabilities, the rubric can be applied without references to AI or humans and could be annotated using humans or a large language model such as GPT4. 16  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Chapter 10 by Robert B. Fisher, Anthony G. Cohn and Christopher Lochhead assesses the current state of the subdomain of computer vision, comprising the full range of image data: static images, videos, multi-spectral images, microscope, ultrasound and medical scanner image. In addition to a five-level scale comparable to other chapters, it developed a five-level “Sophistication” scale to encapsulate the capability range from highly constrained applications to human level and beyond. It offers three analyses of capabilities using the Sophistication scale and then compares the approaches. A discussion of ethical issues arising from use of the scale follows with a focus on development and deployment issues. The final section reflects on three key limitations to the study related to speed, adversaries and explainability. Chapter 11 by Elena Messina presents a five-level scale for evaluating robotic manipulation – from simple pick-and-place operations under controlled conditions to human-level dexterity. It describes how AI-powered hardware and software, including sensing and planning systems, enable progressively more adaptable, flexible and robust manipulation capabilities. The chapter also surveys current benchmarks and competitions, noting they are fragmented and primarily address lower-level skills. It concludes that current robotic manipulation capabilities are broadly at level 2, with ample scope for further development. Chapter 12 by Jean Oh, Cherie Ho, Rebecca Martin and Jonathan Francis proposes a five-level scale for evaluating robotic intelligence, emphasising how robots must combine multiple AI components – including perception, language, planning and ethics – to operate effectively in real-world environments. The chapter details different task complexities, environmental conditions and interaction requirements that define each level. It concludes with recommendations for multi-level benchmarks, offering both a current capability snapshot and a roadmap towards higher-level, fully autonomous robot intelligence. Chapter 13 by Margarita Kalamova and Gianluca Risi introduces a multi-layered framework for analysing how AI capabilities interact with occupations, tasks and education. Centred on the OECD AI Capability Indicators, the chapter outlines methodologies to map AI’s technical progress onto human ability requirements. It proposes both occupation-level and task-level analyses, drawing on O*NET data to align AI functions with detailed descriptors of language, problem solving, perception, social interaction and manipulation. A key innovation is the development of a Catch-Up Index, a quantitative measure of the gap between current AI capabilities and the demands of jobs or tasks, which enables fine-grained analyses of job and educational transformation as a result of AI. Chapter 14 by Ryota Kanai leverages insights from scientific theories of consciousness to develop a five-level scale. Drawing on the author’s own Information Generation Hypothesis, the chapter elaborates on how the hypothesis provides empirically testable functional criteria relevant to AI systems. It explores the evolutionary stages of mind and consciousness, and how the scale can be applied to evaluate existing AI systems. The chapter concludes by reiterating the limitations of the approach, which should be considered exploratory, provisional and reflective of the author's personal stance rather than as a definitive or universally accepted measure. Included as an annex in this chapter are three reviews of the chapter, deanonymised and published with the permission of the authors. They argue against the development of a full indicator of AI consciousness adopting the current approach. # AI Voice Agents in 2025: Smarter, Faster, but Still Not Human

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=96&d=mm&r=g)

**Eugene Datura**
Content Specialist

![](https://d3upe020n1uosc.cloudfront.net/static/web/images/blog/sidebar/sidebar_banner_chatbots_across_customer_channels.png)

In 2025, AI voice agents are more than a tech trend. According to Juniper Research, over 8.4 billion voice-enabled devices are now active globally. That is more than the population of the planet. The global market is projected to exceed $38 billion by 2026. Companies are integrating voice interfaces into hospitals, banks, retail apps, and education platforms.

These systems now book appointments, give financial updates, and help customers shop hands-free. But do they actually improve service or just replace it with automation? The answers are more nuanced than you might expect.

Below is a practical guide to how voice agents work, where they are useful, what problems they face, and how to get started.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/1-2.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/1-2.png)

## What Is a Conversational AI Voice Agent and Why It Matters

A conversational AI voice agent is a program that listens, understands, and responds like a person. It uses speech recognition to hear what you say, natural language processing to understand the meaning, and machine learning to improve over time.

These agents are changing industries where round-the-clock support and speed are essential. In healthcare, they help patients with appointment scheduling and medication reminders. In customer service, they handle routine questions quickly and consistently. Their ability to work without breaks makes them attractive to organizations facing labor shortages.

In the US, the healthcare sector is expected to face a shortage of over 3.2 million workers by 2026, according to the Association of American Medical Colleges. AI agents can help fill these gaps by handling non-urgent interactions.

You can experiment with this kind of technology using the [Graphlogic Text‑to‑Speech API](https://graphlogic.ai/gl-text-to-speech/), which delivers natural-sounding speech suitable for healthcare, finance, or retail use cases.

## How Voice AI Works: Core Technologies Behind the System

Understanding what is under the hood of voice AI systems is key to using them effectively. Each conversation involves several layers of processing that happen in milliseconds.

Systems that combine all of these layers reliably are often built using platforms like the [Graphlogic Voice Box API](https://docs.graphlogic.ai/voice-box-api-245), which lets developers test and refine AI behavior for their audience.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/2-3.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/2-3.png)

## Which Type of Voice Agent Fits Your Use Case

Not every voice system works the same way. Choosing the right type depends on what kind of problem you want to solve.

If your goal is customer-facing automation with some intelligence, start with an AI agent. If your need is internal productivity, consider deploying a copilot-style integration.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/3-1-1024x682.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/3-1-1024x682.png)

## What You Actually Gain from Voice AI

Many companies turn to voice AI because it cuts costs. But its real value goes beyond that. In successful deployments, the technology improves workflow, reduces user frustration, and adds speed to basic interactions.

These results are only possible when the system is trained well and designed around the actual needs of the users.

## Where Voice Agents Actually Work in 2025

Voice AI has moved beyond tech demos. It is now used in major sectors with real-world outcomes.

In healthcare, systems manage patient check-ins, follow-up reminders, and pre-visit screening. The Mayo Clinic’s voice-based assistant is a widely cited example, offering basic health advice and helping reduce hotline load.

In banking, voice agents help with account balances, transaction history, and fraud alerts. Bank of America’s AI assistant “Erica” processed over 1.5 billion interactions by early 2025, with adoption still growing.

In e-commerce, smart assistants guide users through products, manage orders, and even recommend based on past behavior. Retailers using voice interfaces see cart values increase by as much as 18%, according to internal case studies from Salesforce.

In education, tools like Duolingo have added spoken comprehension testing and pronunciation scoring, improving retention and engagement.

These sectors succeed with voice AI because they focus on repeatable, time-sensitive tasks that do not require emotional nuance.

## Why Voice AI Still Struggles in Some Areas

No technology is perfect, and voice AI comes with limits. These are especially important in sectors like healthcare and finance where precision matters.

Systems often struggle with:

To make sure your implementation succeeds, test systems with real users early. Also ensure your platform provider follows encryption and security protocols.

Even the most advanced platforms will misfire without good training data. That is why tools like the [Graphlogic Generative AI Platform](https://graphlogic.ai/generative-ai/) are useful. They support retrieval-augmented generation and domain-specific fine-tuning for more accurate results.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/4.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/4.png)

## What the Next Generation of Voice AI Will Look Like

By late 2025, voice AI is evolving beyond basic assistants into a more adaptive and multimodal experience. This shift is driven by user demand for smoother, more human-like interaction, as well as by improvements in model training and deployment tools.

Here are some of the main trends shaping the future of voice AI:

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/5.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/5.png)

### Industry Forecasts for 2026 and Beyond

Looking ahead, several forecasts outline where this market is going:

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/6-2.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/6-2.png)

The takeaway is simple. Voice AI is not just growing. It is being embedded into critical systems that need accuracy, speed, and reliability. Platforms like the [Graphlogic Generative AI Platform](https://graphlogic.ai/generative-ai/) are already incorporating retrieval-augmented generation and real-time adaptation to meet these rising expectations.

Businesses that ignore voice AI risk falling behind, especially as users expect seamless, voice-enabled support as the default — not the exception.

Echoes of Privacy: Uncovering the Profiling Practices of Voice Assistants Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh University of Southern California Los Angeles, California, USA khezresm@usc.edu Elaine Zhu Northeastern University Boston, Massachusetts, USA zhu.lae@northeastern.edu Kiersten Grieco Northeastern University Boston, Massachusetts, USA grieco.k@northeastern.edu Daniel J. Dubois Northeastern University Boston, Massachusetts, USA d.dubois@northeastern.edu Konstantinos Psounis University of Southern California Los Angeles, California, USA kpsounis@usc.edu David Choffnes Northeastern University Boston, Massachusetts, USA choffnes@ccs.neu.edu Abstract Many companies, including Google, Amazon, and Apple, offer voice assistants as a convenient solution for answering general voice queries and accessing their services. These voice assistants have gained popularity and can be easily accessed through various smart devices such as smartphones, smart speakers, smartwatches, and an increasing array of other devices. However, this convenience comes with potential privacy risks. For instance, while companies vaguely mention in their privacy policies that they may use voice interactions for user profiling, it remains unclear to what extent this profiling occurs and whether voice interactions pose greater privacy risks compared to other interaction modalities.
In this paper, we conduct 1,171 experiments involving 24,530 queries with different personas and interaction modalities during 20 months to characterize how the three most popular voice assistants profile their users. We analyze factors such as labels assigned to users, their accuracy, the time taken to assign these labels, differ-ences between voice and web interactions, and the effectiveness of profiling remediation tools offered by each voice assistant. Our findings reveal that profiling can happen without interaction, can be incorrect and inconsistent at times, may take several days or weeks to change, and is affected by the interaction modality.
Keywords privacy, profiling, persona, voice assistant 1 Introduction Voice assistants, including Amazon Alexa [5], Google Assistant [34], and Apple Siri [11], have rapidly gained popularity as versatile tools for accessing information and services, reducing the need for tradi-tional physical interfaces, with more than 142 million users in the US alone [58]. Despite their convenience, voice assistants still raise concerns regarding user privacy, mirroring issues found in other non-vocal interaction modalities such as web browsing. In the absence of clear disclosures and explicit consumer consent, such profiling constitutes privacy invasion, as it relies on surveillance of consumers’ online activities to produce revenue (e.g., via ads). Additionally, recent findings have revealed that certain interactions with third-party skills of the Alexa voice assistant are utilized for profiling purposes [39]. However, as far as we know, it remains uncertain whether and how voice assis-tants themselves, without utilizing third-party skills, engage in user profiling. Further, the extent to which their profiling methods resemble or differ from other interaction modalities, along with the associated privacy implications, remains unclear.
This highlights the necessity for further privacy research to explore this topic and offer transparency regarding how voice assis-tants profile their users. Profiling information becomes integrated into the user’s data and can have various ramifications, including impacting the user experience by potentially leading to the dis-play of irrelevant advertisements. Additionally, it can influence sponsoring contracts, such as determining inclusion or exclusion from relevant promotional campaigns. Moreover, there is a risk of unwanted or incorrect information being shared with third parties, highlighting the need to understand and address the potential side effects of user profiling in this new context.
The goal of this research is to shed light on the privacy im-plications due to interactions with voice assistants. This includes investigating the scope, accuracy, and timing of profiling, such as what aspects are being profiled and whether this profiling is pertinent. Additionally, the research will explore differences in pro-filing between voice interactions and other modalities, such as web browsing, to understand if and how the methods diverge. Finally, we will analyze the effectiveness of the profiling mitigation tools offered by each voice assistant such as opt-out mechanisms and the possibility to delete or rectify incorrect labels.
Unfortunately, attaining such a goal is challenging because the most popular voice assistants are not software that runs on users’ premises, but instead they operate as cloud services, making it very difficult to audit their internal operations. While the privacy policies of these platforms disclose the potential for user profiling based on voice interactions [3, 12, 35], they typically lack details on the methodology involved. Fortunately, privacy regulations in certain jurisdictions (e.g., GDPR [28] and CCPA [56]) compel these platforms to allow users to make data disclosure requests [4, 13, 36].

Through these requests, platforms are required to provide users with all the information they have collected or generated, including user profiles, often described in terms of demographic (e.g., income group) and interest labels (e.g., an interest in cars).
To address the challenge above and achieve our goal, we de-veloped a rigorous experimental methodology and applied it to the three most prevalent voice assistant platforms: Google Assis-tant [34], Alexa [5], and Siri [11]. Our approach involves the creation of new user accounts, each meticulously trained with a curated set of voice queries designed to simulate various user personas, each one with an expected set of target profiling labels. Then, we lever-age the data disclosure features inherent to each voice assistant platform to monitor the appearance of actual profiling labels. For instance, if an account is trained to mimic a “luxury persona” with questions tailored around luxury topics, we anticipate the emer-gence of labels aligned with this persona, such as “high income.” After applying this methodology to the three platforms above and completing 1,171 experiments with a total of 24,530 voice queries over the course of 20 months, we discovered that Apple Siri does not produce profiling labels, while in the remaining platforms profiling does occur and can be erroneous and inconsistent at times.
For example, we have seen situations in which profiling happens without any user interactions, resulting in arbitrary profiling labels (Google Assistant). Moreover, the process of profiling varied signif-icantly in accuracy and duration, with unexpected labels appearing (Google Assistant), different labels following the same questions at different times (Google Assistant), and profiling labels taking days to appear (Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa). Importantly, we observed that the interaction modality can influence the accuracy and timing of profiling, with different profiling outcomes depending on whether the interaction occurs via voice commands or through the web (Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa). Finally, we tested the mitigation tools each platform offered and whether any label rectification or opt-out request was correctly fulfilled.
Summarizing, the contributions of this paper are the following: (1) a new persona-based methodology for producing profiling labels in different voice assistant platforms (Section 4), (2) a characterization of voice assistant first-party profiling across several dimensions, such as accuracy and timing (Sec-tions 5.1 and 5.2), along with an understanding of how plat-forms pre-populate profiling labels on fresh accounts.
(3) a comparison of profiling across different interaction modal-ities (Section 5.3), (4) an assessment of the efficacy of mitigation mechanism such as profiling opt-out and label rectification (5.4).
To ensure reproducibility and enable new research, we made our research artifacts, including code and datasets, publicly available at: https://github.com/NEU-SNS/voice-assistants-pets25.git.
2 Related Work Voice assistant privacy. Voice assistants and the devices typically used to access them (e.g., smart speakers) have raised privacy and security concerns, as discussed in several recent surveys [24, 44, 63].
A large amount of existing privacy research focuses on risks that are likely due to technological limitations such as smart speakers misactivations [27, 32], unintentional software bugs that some-times led to unauthorized sharing of voice recordings [19, 31, 54], and other instances of data exposure due to third-party apps or skills [23, 39, 64]. Another line of work has shown that it is possible to infer user labels from the characteristics of the recording instead of just from its transcription [55], thus creating more profiling op-portunities for voice assistant vendors. While these works focus on important risks, we are complementary with respect to them since we focus on the measurement and mitigation of intentional data collection in terms of profiling labels to the first party (i.e., the voice assistant vendor). Specifically, we focus on targeting the labels of each specific platform using explicitly biased utterances while maintaining voice characteristics as neutral as possible.
Persona-based inference of labels. In this work, we use a persona-based methodology to produce labeling in the context of voice assistants and then use data disclosure requests to obtain user labels.
This methodology was inspired by the ones used in a large body of prior work (e.g., [1, 14–16, 20, 26, 29, 43]), where different synthetic profiles (personas) are used to study how data is propagated to third parties in contexts such as the web and mobile apps. These works typically use personas to determine what data is shared with third parties [29], server-side data exchanges [16, 26], and other online tracking and advertising behavior [1, 20, 43]. Although our work also uses a persona-based approach, a limitation of most existing work is that it focuses on limited modalities (e.g., the web) that do not include voice assistant. One recent persona-based work [39] focuses on voice assistants, but it has a different scope with respect to ours since it is limited to third-party skills, it only focuses on the Alexa voice assistant, it does not target the voice assistant vendor itself (i.e., the first party), and obtains labeling data indirectly and in a probabilistic way through the analysis of the ads ecosystem rather than using deterministic data disclosure requests as we do.
Other labeling determination approaches. Prior work in the broader context of Internet of Things (IoT), including smart speakers, has traditionally addressed the labeling problem by understanding what data is shared to their cloud platforms (both belonging to the de-vice’s vendor and to third parties). This has been typically done by relying on device modification or logging capabilities of specific platforms [22, 33, 40, 62]. Other work used black-box experiments to identify how the viewing habits gathered by smart TVs [30, 45] and smart speakers interactions [39] were shared with advertisers.
Finally, other studies that focus on web [18] and mobile apps [49] have relied on instrumentation [37, 50], automation, and network traffic interception [51, 52] not available in the context of voice assistants. In this work, we specifically address voice assistants, which are cloud services accessed through smart speakers or apps, and not devices themselves. Moreover, profile inference typically happens in the cloud and not the device itself. For this reason, we cannot use device modification or network traffic analysis as done in prior related work. Similarly to some of the work above, we use a black-box approach, where we only access entry points (i.e., our voice queries) and exit points (i.e., user labels) from data disclosure requests mandated by law. The main difference is that we do not rely on third parties such as advertisers, since we target first-party (i.e., vendor) labels and not how such labels are shared or used.
72 Echoes of Privacy Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2025(2) 3 Context, Definitions, and Goals We now describe the context, definitions, and goals of this work.
3.1 Context The integration of voice assistants into daily life has revolutionized how we interact with technology, offering convenience and effi-ciency in performing a wide array of tasks. However, this interaction brings significant privacy implications, particularly concerning the profiling capabilities of these systems. Profiling by voice assistants involves analyzing voice commands, searches, and interactions to construct detailed profiles of users [3, 12, 35]. These profiles can reveal private personal information, including demographic details, that users might prefer to keep confidential [4, 13, 36].
The implications of such unintentional data sharing are multi-faceted. Firstly, there is the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information, where personal data could be exposed to third parties or inadvertently leaked through security breaches [19, 31, 54]. Sec-ondly, the demographic and personal information obtained from interactions can be used to tailor marketing efforts in a highly targeted, and potentially intrusive, manner [39].
Even though users, thanks to privacy laws [28, 56], can now access their profile and even opt out [4, 13, 36], the opaque nature of data processing and profiling practices by voice assistant providers complicates users’ ability to control what information is collected about them and how it is used [41]. Many users are unaware of the extent to which their data contributes to their digital profile or the ways in which this profile influences their interactions with technology and content online [42, 46, 60].
Understanding the privacy implications of interacting with voice assistants is important for recognizing the potential risks to per-sonal privacy. It highlights the importance of transparent data practices, robust privacy settings, and the need for users to be in-formed and cautious about the information they share through these increasingly ubiquitous services.
3.2 Definitions In the context of our study on the privacy implications and user profiling capabilities of voice assistant platforms, we refine our definitions to ensure clarity and precision in our analysis.
Voice assistants. We define voice assistants as software compo-nents designed to interpret and execute voice commands, enabling them to perform various tasks. Voice assistants can receive voice in-puts from users and provide audible feedback or take actions based on the analysis of these inputs. The voice assistants we consider in this study, selected based on their popularity in the US [57], are the following: Google Assistant [34], Alexa [5], and Siri [11]. All these voice assistants are cloud-based, meaning that the user-controlled devices used to access them (e.g., smart speakers) simply forward the recordings to them, with the processing (and profiling) happen-ing in the cloud. This process is typically detailed in the privacy policies pages of each voice assistant.
Profiling labels. We define profiling labels as the key compo-nents within a user profile, derived from user data and interactions with the voice assistants. These labels demonstrate specific charac-teristics that distinguish users from one another. We categorized them into two types: demographic and interest labels. Demographic labels capture the user’s demographic attributes, such as relation-ship status, educational background, etc. These labels can either be based on explicit user data or be derived from user’s interactions.
In contrast, interest labels offer insights into the user’s preferences and interests in products or ad categories. These labels usually are inferred from the user’s interactions. Both types of labels enable personalized experiences and targeted content delivery.
Persona. A key aspect of our experimental methodology is to train voice assistant user accounts as a certain persona. Taking inspiration from previous work [1, 14–16, 20, 26, 29, 43], we con-ceptualize a persona as a composite profile consisting of one or more specific profiling labels that collectively define the perceived characteristics, preferences, or demographic details of a user as interpreted by a voice assistant. To construct a specific persona with targeted labels, we curate a series of tailored queries and ask them to the voice assistant. For instance, one might create a per-sona in Google’s ecosystem that is identified as “Single” or “Renter,” or in Amazon’s ecosystem as having an interest in “Fashion.” The definition of a persona is contingent upon the profiling mechanisms of each voice assistant, which use interaction data to assign labels according to their user characterization methods.
Training queries. We define training queries as a curated set of queries intentionally designed to shape or guide the development of a targeted persona. The purpose of these queries is to direct the profiling algorithms of the voice assistant toward converging on a specific label that accurately reflects the intended persona.
Modalities of interaction. We define modalities of interaction as the interaction methods through which users can access informa-tion from each voice assistant company. These interactions can occur through voice inputs via voice assistant interfaces or text-based queries on web interfaces. Note that we do not distinguish modalities between vocal voice assistant interactions and textual non-web voice assistant interactions using accessible interfaces de-signed for people who cannot speak, since during our preliminary experiments, we observed that such interactions are processed in the same way and produce the same results (Appendix B.3).
3.3 Goals The goal of this study is to explore if and how voice assistants profile their users with labels—both demographic (e.g., “Married”) and interest-based (e.g., “Fashion”). Specifically, we will address the following research questions (RQ): RQ1. Before experimentation, does the voice assistant have any prepopulated labels?
This research question aims to determine if the system begins with any predefined labels on newly created accounts before any inter-action with the system. Having wrong initial labels may affect user experience (e.g., irrelevant recommendations) and mislead adver-tisers, with the potential of wrong labels being propagated to third parties. We address this question by creating 200 accounts, and then waiting for labels to appear.
RQ2. After experimentation, does profiling actually happen and to what extent?
We aim to quantify the extent of user profiling by voice assistants in terms of accuracy and consistency, assessing the depth and breadth 73 Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2025(2) Khezresmaeilzadeh et al.
of data collection. The purpose is to improve transparency over pro-filing practices. To answer this question, we perform 460 persona-based voice interaction large-scale experiments using 19 different personas for Google, 7 for Amazon, and 5 for Apple (see Section 4 for a detailed description of our experiments and justification for the selected number of personas per platform).
RQ3. Does the interaction modality affect profiling?
This question investigates whether different modalities of interac-tion (e.g., web vs. voice) have distinct impacts on the scope and accuracy of user profiling. This is important to understand whether users are profiled (or misprofiled) differently when accessing infor-mation through a voice assistant with respect to another modality such as the web. To achieve this goal, we perform web persona-based experiments performing the same queries, but with a different modality, and then compare the results with our voice results.
RQ4. Are the opt-out options provided by these platforms effective?
This research question focuses on identifying whether the current strategies to mitigate the privacy risks associated with user profiling by voice assistants are sufficient enough to protect users from being misprofiled or from being profiled against their will. To answer it we investigate whether we can effectively remove or change profil-ing labels from our persona accounts and the level of granularity (e.g., partial vs. complete opt-out). In the next sections, we detail the methodology employed to investigate these RQs (Section 4), followed by an analysis of the findings (Section 5), and a discussion on the implications of our results (Section 6).
3.4 Ethics This research project involves only the authors of the paper and their direct collaborators listed in the acknowledgment section; no external research subjects were recruited. The experiments were meticulously performed one at a time to minimize any disruption or disturbance to the voice assistants being tested. While Google, Amazon, and Apple prohibit misrepresentation (such as using fake data), these rules primarily target activities that harm or affect other users, such as fraud, impersonation, or identity misrepresentation.
Our experiments did not impact other users or disrupt services and did not involve fraud. Our approach aligns with established practices in similar studies, see, for example, [2, 17, 21, 25].
We did not need to disclose our findings with the companies hosting the voice assistants since their privacy policies already acknowledge the profiling activities associated with their services.
Instead, our focus has been to provide greater transparency regard-ing these profiling activities and their implications for privacy.

4.1 Testing Environment Our testing environment, located in the United States, for evaluating voice assistant devices comprises three main components: (i) the voice assistant platforms being tested; (ii) a PC equipped with a Python script to automate the playback of audio recordings; and (iii) a pair of non-smart speakers connected to the PC, tasked with playing the recordings to the voice assistant.
To access Google, Alexa, and Siri voice assistants, we used both smart speakers and smart phones/tablets. (In preliminary testing, we found that profiling labels remained consistent regardless of de-vice type, and thus likely have no impact on profiling.) Specifically, we use the following voice-assistant enabled devices: • Google Assistant Access: (i) 3 iPhone 7 devices running iOS 15.8.3, (ii) 1 iPhone 8 running iOS 16.7.8, and (iii) 1 iPhone 13 running iOS 16.0. The Google Home app version on all iPhones was 1.9.115.901.
• Alexa Access: (i) 1 Amazon Echo Dot (1st generation), (ii) 3 Amazon Echo Dot (3rd gen.), and (iii) 1 Amazon Echo Dot (5th gen.). The Alexa Home app was installed on an iPhone 13 Pro running iOS 17.5.1, with Alexa app version 2024.15.
• Siri Access: 1 iPhone 13 Pro Max running iOS 16.0.
For each voice assistant, we created distinct personas, each asso-ciated with a persona-specific set of English training queries. To guarantee the consistency of our experiments across multiple ac-counts of a persona, we pre-recorded the queries we intended to ask the voice assistants using the voice of one of the authors. Then, we developed an automated Python script to systematically play back these recordings. The process involves the script first triggering the voice assistant device’s wake word (e.g., “Hey Siri”), followed by a single query. It then pauses for a one-minute interval, which during preliminary testing proved to be a sufficient window for all our voice assistants to process and respond to the query. Upon completion of this interval, the script proceeds to play the next query. During the whole experimentation, we manually supervised the automatic execution of the experiments to ensure that the voice assistant under test always activates (i.e., it recognizes the wake word) and always understands the voice query correctly (i.e., its answers are relevant to the questions). This methodical approach ensures our experiments are repeatable under identical conditions.
4.2 Experiment Preparation To ensure that our results accurately reflected the profiling behav-ior of voice assistants without the influence of external variables, we adopted a rigorous method to maintain the independence and isolation of each device and account. While we cannot guarantee perfect isolation, our method constitutes a best effort to control as many relevant factors as possible.
For each voice assistant platform, we created several fresh ac-counts (one for each persona instantiation) using the Chrome web browser (due to its popularity [59], and likely use by many con-sumers) in private mode to minimize the chances of being tracked.
Since the account creation process required a phone number for SMS verification, we obtained a new non-VoIP phone number for each account to ensure independence. Each phone number was used only once per platform, so no two accounts shared the same phone number. By using a browser in private mode and by not reusing phone numbers across accounts within the same platform, we minimize any potential cross-contamination of data or profiling influences that could compromise the integrity of the experiment.
Additionally, we reset the device used to factory settings to access the voice assistant before logging in with a fresh account.
This ensured that no residual data from the previous account could influence the voice assistant’s behavior.
Finally, to prevent our IP address from affecting the profiling pro-cess, we connected the smart devices used to access voice assistants through a VPN using the same IP address for all experiments, thus ensuring that any observed differences in profiling were attribut-able to the interactions specific to each account and not to external network factors. Each persona in our study had unique behaviors, and our results showed distinct profiling outcomes across personas, with no evidence of cross-contamination. Thus we have evidence that profiling differences were driven by each account’s unique interactions, rather than any influence from shared IP usage.
4.3 Common Experimental Approach We employed a common experimental approach across all the voice assistants we tested, as explained below. The following subsections highlight the specific variations in our methodology tailored to each voice assistant.
4.3.1 Profiling and Data Access. Our study began with determining which profiling labels are observable and how they can be accessed on each platform. Since each platform employs different approaches to categorize user information, we systematically searched for acces-sible profiling labels on each, exploring their data access tools and documentation to prepare for evaluating their profiling behaviors.
4.3.2 Persona Choices. After identifying the accessible profiling labels of each system, we designed personas, each targeting a spe-cific profiling label. This strategy enabled us to develop tailored queries that guide the system towards recognizing each profiling label, and allowed us to study the system’s behavior for each label.
For each platform, we first identified the possible profiling labels and then created a distinct persona for each label. For each persona, we created 10 accounts per persona to ensure a meaningful sample size while efficiently managing computational resources and time constraints. Previous studies in similar contexts have shown that 10 samples per persona are sufficient to detect consistent patterns and trends (shown in Appendix B.2 and B.3).
4.3.3 Query Choices. To develop the queries for our experiments, we employed prompt engineering with the goal of generating rele-vant questions that align with typical user interactions and engage 75 Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2025(2) Khezresmaeilzadeh et al.
with each voice assistant’s profiling system. We first used ChatGPT-4o [47] to assist in the process of query generation, ensuring that the queries were not influenced by the biases of the authors. We then carefully reviewed and manually refined the queries based on consensus among the authors. The ChatGPT-4 prompts were crafted with trial and error, using direct, concise instructions with relevant keywords to clearly convey the profiling labels and ensure consistency across different personas. The tailored prompts used for this purpose are included in Appendix A.
4.3.4 Waiting Periods. Based on our preliminary experiments (Ap-pendix B.2), we implemented an initial “prepopulation” one-week waiting period to allow any prepopulated labels to appear, as we observed that these labels typically emerge within this timeframe.
This approach also enabled us to identify any pre-existing labels, ensuring that we excluded accounts where the target label was already present from the corresponding experiments.
After this initial waiting period, we deployed a set of training queries to trigger account profiling. Profiling by the voice assistants is not immediate either, and each platform requires a “profiling” waiting period before profiling labels start becoming observable.
We determined this waiting period experimentally, and chose a standardized one-week waiting period for all platforms. This deci-sion was informed by our preliminary experiments conducted in the Spring and Fall of 2023 (see Section 4.7), which indicated that profiling labels typically emerge within this timeframe (by 5.9 days for Google, and by 5.5 days for Alexa).
In our most recent, large-scale experiments, we observed that profiling happened slower than in our preliminary experiments (see Section 5 and more specifically Figure 2). Motivated by this, if some target labels were not achieved within the initial one-week period, we generated a new set of queries using the prompts described in Appendix A and waited for a new one-week period before re-observing the profiles. We continued this monitoring process for a total of four weeks, at which point we observed that profiles were stabilized. (This approach additionally helped maintain consistent interaction levels, reducing the risk of accounts being flagged due to insufficient activity.) 4.3.5 Modality Experiments. Profiling via web and voice modality could be similar, given that transcripts of voice interactions can be used similarly to web input. Investigating the nature of this similarity is important, both to understand relevant privacy impli-cations and because consumers may have different expectations from different modalities [48]. To assess the impact of different interaction modes on user profiling, we conducted experiments using two querying methods: web searches and voice commands.
For each service, we replicated persona experiments using a web browser, logged into new accounts, and compared the results to those obtained via voice interactions. This reveals how each modal-ity influences the creation and updating of user profiles.
4.3.6 Mitigation Experiments. We conducted mitigation experi-ments beginning with accounts associated with personas that had successfully reached their target profiling labels. Once these ac-counts have been profiled, we opted out the accounts to stop data collection and profiling. Later, we opted the accounts back in and monitored their profiles over time to see if opting out had a lasting impact on the system’s ability to profile based on past interactions.
In the rest of the paper, for experiment counting purposes, we count account actions, such as checking for prepopulated labels in an account (RQ1), asking a batch of queries to an account (RQ2, RQ3), and opting out of profiling for an account (RQ4), as one experiment each.
4.4 Google Assistant Experiments 4.4.1 Profiling and Data Access. Google’s ad personalization strat-egy utilizes comprehensive user interaction data from its services and it enables users to modify their advertisement preferences in their Google Account settings [35]. Google categorizes this infor-mation into multiple demographic categories, outlined as follows: • Relationship: whether the user is single, married, etc.
• Household Income: estimated income bracket.
• Education: highest level of education achieved.
• Industry: sector of employment.
• Employer Size: rough size of the user’s place of employment.
• Homeownership: whether the user owns or rents their home.
• Parenting: whether the user has children.
Each of the above demographic categories has several possi-ble options referred to as profiling labels. Google allows users to view their profiling labels in real-time through its My Ad Center interface [36], encompassing services like Google Assistant.
In addition to demographic categories, Google also profiles users based on interest labels (as defined in Section 3.2). We monitored the impact of interactions on the generation of these interest labels by systematically reviewing the My Ad Center interface [36] over a 4-week period. However, we did not observe any evidence of interest labels being assigned through interactions with Google As-sistant, suggesting that Google likely does not derive interest labels from voice interactions. Consequently, we focused our analysis of Google profiling on demographic labels, as they were the only ones demonstrably affected by voice interactions.
4.4.2 Persona Choices. Given Google’s demographic-based profil-ing system, our selection process for personas included all possible demographic labels to ensure comprehensive targeting 1. We con-sidered each label as a potential persona. This allowed us to create a set of 19 distinct personas for Google profiling experiments.
4.4.3 Query Choices. For Google-specific experiments, we tailored prompts specifically for Google Assistant to align with Google’s profiling system. The prompt used for this purpose is included in Appendix A.1. For each persona (profiling label), ten distinct Google account samples were created. We designed 20 queries for each profiling label. This number was chosen as it was sufficient to trigger the target profiling labels based on insights from prelimi-nary experiments (Appendix B.2). This allowed us to systematically evaluate the impact of query type on Google’s profiling accuracy.
4.4.4 Mitigation Experiments. In addition to opting-out, we also investigated the ability to selectively amend and delete labels offered by Google. In this case, our methodology does not include a waiting period since label deletion and editing are processed immediately (i.e., the change is immediately visible in Google My Ad Center [36]).
