Recruitment and pre-workshop questionnaire 186  9 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Executive summary Depending on the source, artificial intelligence (AI) is either set to save the world or destroy it. In a landscape dominated by hype and fear, clear, reliable and nuanced information about the true capabilities of AI remains strikingly absent. Even AI developers do not understand the current capacities of AI systems – or how rapidly they are advancing. As an independent and authoritative international body, the OECD is well positioned to fill this knowledge gap. Drawing on its experience in comparative assessment, extensive collaboration with leading computer scientists and engineers, and its international perspective, the OECD has developed a unique methodology to deliver rigorous, evidence-based and clear insights into the real-world performance of AI. This framework is known as the OECD AI Capability Indicators. It offers policy makers the clarity they urgently need to navigate an increasingly complex technological environment and craft informed, future-proof strategies. Following the introduction, this technical report comprises three chapters written by the AI and Future of Skills project, describing the development and limitations of the current scales. The proceeding nine chapters are technical reports for each of nine beta indicators: language; social interaction; problem solving; creativity; knowledge, learning and memory; metacognition and critical thinking; vision; manipulation; and robotic intelligence. In Chapter 13, possible methods for leveraging the indicators for analyses of tasks and occupations are also considered. The final chapter introduces a tenth indicator, consciousness, which was also developed but not released as a beta indicator as the ethical and social questions of consciousness in AI remain controversial. It is not yet clear whether the indicator will be reworked or completely excluded going forward. In the meantime, the OECD shares lessons learnt from the experience, as well as key comments from the reviewers, to further the discussion and develop the necessary consensus. The ten indicators featured in this volume cover a range of human abilities that each describe the development of AI towards full human equivalence. The indicators are presented as five-level scales, where the most challenging capabilities for AI systems are found towards the top. Each level includes a short description of the sorts of capabilities that AI systems at that level can perform accurately and consistently. The rating of current AI performance on each scale is linked to available evidence. The indicators are being published in beta form with an invitation for two critical groups of stakeholders to provide feedback: computer scientists, whose AI evaluation work provides the evidence for the indicators, and policy makers, whose ability to interpret and leverage the insights from the scales is critical for the development of informed decisions. The OECD will release the first full version of the indicators after feedback from stakeholders and the development of a systematic updating protocol. The indicators were developed over five years, drawing on a large network on AI researchers, psychologists and other experts. The chapters of this technical report were written by 32 experts and reviewed by another 25 experts. A shorter and more accessible overview of the indicators, which comprises a brief overview of the methodological approach to their development, has been published separately.
10  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Abel Baret, OECD Sam Mitchell, OECD Stuart Elliott, OECD The arrival of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI) systems in recent years highlights the need for new tools to monitor their rapid development. This opening chapter introduces the rationale for a new framework to help policy makers and researchers understand the true extent of AI capabilities and how they compare to human abilities. The chapter discusses how the indicators can be used to support analyses related to larger ethical and safety issues related to AI use; evaluation of the impact of AI on the workforce and the economy; and the impact of AI on education. After outlining the subsequent 13 chapters, it invites collaboration with the computer science and human psychology communities to strengthen the indicators into a precise and responsive policy tool that can capture the critical implications of future AI developments. 1 Introduction  11 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Introduction Depending on the source, artificial intelligence (AI)1 is either set to save the world or destroy it. In a landscape dominated by hype and fear, clear, reliable and nuanced information about the true capabilities of AI remains strikingly absent. Even AI developers do not understand the current capacities of AI systems. With the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, AI and robotics are rapidly advancing, and policy makers worldwide recognise the need to assess their capability. In 2024, the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine revisited its 2017 review of Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work. It observed that policy makers still lack the information about AI capabilities that is needed to guide policy. Meanwhile, the AI Act of the European Union has called for its newly created AI Office to regularly monitor AI capabilities (EUR-Lex, 2024[1]). For their part, the OECD Council’s AI Recommendation and the Statement of the 2025 Paris AI Summit (OECD Legal Instruments, 2024[2]; La Maison Élysée, 2025[3]) emphasise the importance of understanding AI’s influence on the job market. Internationally, policy makers have already acknowledged the importance of a clear understanding of AI capabilities for their work. However, without an evidence-based framework describing what AI can do, it will be impossible to respond appropriately to either questions of AI ethics and safety, or its impact on education or jobs. While technical initiatives (MLCommons, 2025[4]; PAI, n.d.[5]) seek to quantify the computing efficiency of models, no equivalent effort has analysed what these models can and cannot do. As an independent and authoritative international body, the OECD is well positioned to fill this knowledge gap. Drawing on its experience of comparative assessment, extensive collaboration with leading computer scientists and engineers, and its international perspective, the OECD has developed a unique methodology to deliver rigorous, evidence-based and clear insights into the real-world performance of AI. This framework, developed within the AI and Future Skills project, is known as the AI Capability Indicators. It offers policy makers and researchers the clarity they urgently need to understand the true extent of AI capabilities and how they compare to human abilities.2 The initial result of this framework, the OECD’s beta AI Capability Indicators are presented here. OECD (2023[6]) identified four criteria for effective indicators of AI capabilities: 1. Understandable: They should be easy to interpret. They should communicate current strengths and limitations of AI in a straightforward manner and should be understandable to non-experts. This implies, among other things, there should only be a few of them. 2. Policy relevant: They should enable policy makers to draw conclusions about AI’s impact on education, employment and the economy. 3. Comprehensive: They should cover all key aspects of AI capabilities needed to understand their implications. 4. Responsive: They should indicate important developments in AI, which means they will have to be systematically updated at regular intervals. Linking AI capabilities to human abilities allows policy makers to gauge AI’s potential role in education, work and everyday life. Existing frameworks that characterise AI capabilities such as MLCommons (MLCommons, 2025[4]) and Stanford’s AI Index (Maslej et al., 2025[5]) discuss capabilities purely in terms of benchmark performance without any comparison to human abilities. Taken in isolation, benchmark results are unclear to non-AI experts, and even to AI researchers it is unclear how results relate to AI systems’ capacity to perform tasks in real-world situations. In a discussion of the limitations of current AI benchmarks, the authors of the 2025 AI Index report noted that “(t)o truly assess the capabilities of AI systems, more rigorous and comprehensive evaluations are needed” (Maslej et al., 2025[7]) The OECD’s framework is unique in its effort to compare AI capabilities to the full range of human abilities used in the job market, recognising that in many cases adequate AI 12  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 benchmarks for the advanced levels are still lacking. The indicators provide a conceptual framework for identifying or developing tests that can evaluate AI’s capabilities systematically across the full range of human skill domains relevant to life and employment. Frameworks based in AI performance on benchmarks without a human baseline risk being quickly overtaken by rapid AI developments. An additional benefit of grounding a framework to evaluate AI capabilities in human abilities is they are relatively fixed over time. In other words, the framework will remain stable and informative amid rapid AI progress until it truly surpasses the full range of human performance. Anthropic’s AI Economic Index (Handa et al., 2025[8]) adopted a novel approach to analysing the impact of AI developments on the economy by linking Claude.ai’s capabilities to some human tasks. This was performed by analysing millions of interactions between Claude large language models (LLMs) and users where tasks that could be linked to those found on the O*NET (a United States–based database that systematically describes the skills, tasks, and requirements of different occupations) were performed. However, this approach was limited to analyses of chat-based interactions with LLMs. As such, it did not aim to compare AI performance to the full range of human abilities used in occupations. To make our indicators understandable and relevant for policy makers, AI capabilities are linked to the human abilities familiar to the policy community. This approach achieves comprehensiveness by covering a wide range of AI and robotic systems, inclusive of but not limited to large language models (LLMs) and other forms of generative AI. The capabilities of these systems are also compared to the full range of human abilities. The OECD is committed to developing a feasible way to update the indicators at regular intervals to reflect significant developments in the state of the art. A request for help from the expert community Given the beta form of the indicators, the OECD needs continued collaboration with the computer scientists and policy makers. The indicators need to be strengthened to become a precise and responsive policy tool that can capture the critical implications of future AI developments. The beta status of the scales is thus a direct request to the expert community: If you think something is wrong with the current version of the scales, tell us how they need to be fixed. Example use cases The OECD is developing the AI Capability Indicators as a foundation for a range of policy analyses related to the implications of AI. Before introducing the scales and how they were developed in more detail, the report discusses how the indicators can be used to support analyses related to 1) larger ethical and safety issues related to AI use; 2) evaluation of the impact of AI on the workforce and the economy; and 3) the impact of AI on education. Proposals for how to develop the last two type of analyses using the indicators are outlined in Chapter 13. Using the indicators to analyse AI’s implications for jobs and the economy The indicators offer a framework to evaluate how AI affects our economies. One approach to the impact of AI on the labour market is to map AI capabilities to the tasks humans perform at work, which can provide insights into potential shifts in job roles. This provides the starting point for analyses related to AI’s implications for jobs and the economy, especially those occupations at risk of substantial levels of automation. This research could be analysed in a variety of ways to derive estimates for individual occupations, which could then be aggregated to support analyses for the overall economy.  13 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Chapter 13 describes the way the indicators can be linked to the ability demands of different occupations and tasks and proposes a methodology for constructing an AI Catch-up Index for a fine-grained analyses of job transformation as a result of AI. As the indicators are updated in future, the potential implications for specific occupations and the overall economy can then be directly in line with the latest ratings. With the link from the AI Capability Indicators to the implications for different occupations, policy makers could analyse the potential sensitivity of the results to changes in specific AI capabilities. This will make it possible to identify AI capabilities that should be tracked closely given their larger implications for employment. Of course, even if it is technologically possible to partially automate different occupations, AI may not necessarily be used to displace workers. Specific practical barriers to AI application may only be apparent from a more detailed analysis. Alternatively, the potential use of AI may be more expensive than people continuing to perform the function. This might be the case if the automatable task represents only a small part of an overall occupation and the resulting benefits are small. There might also be ethical or safety concerns with substituting AI for humans in particular types of tasks. The indicators do not address potential barriers to using AI. Rather, they provide a signal that AI could carry out substantial portions of occupations or tasks. This, in turn, invites an examination of whether other factors are likely to encourage or discourage the use of those capabilities. The AI Capability Indicators could also be used as a framework for monitoring the diffusion and application of AI. This would reveal whether the diffusion process changes as AI capabilities increase and begin to approach full human equivalence in different areas. Using the indicators to analyse AI’s implications for education The AI Capability Indicators can also be used to support policy conversations related to education. The indicators can help inform two primary sets of policy questions: 1) the use of AI to carry out instructional and administrative activities; and 2) appropriate learning goals for students. These two questions have different facets. The AI Capability Indicators, for example, can be used to consider how AI capabilities relate to the ability demands for teachers. How will AI affect the range of tasks currently undertaken by teachers? Questions related to AI’s implications for the appropriate learning goals for students also relates in part to the occupational analyses in the previous section. In broad strokes, large-scale shifts in the workforce are expected with potential transformations in the human role in carrying out tasks. These provide a picture of how abilities needed by adults are likely to evolve with greater AI capabilities. Although the picture is described in terms of the workplace, many tasks appear both inside and outside of work. This transformation poses challenges to the education sector in considering how to prepare students for their adult lives. What skills will students need as AI acquires more complex human capabilities. Should students continue to learn skills that AI already has? Are there skills that should be preserved for their intrinsic human value, regardless of their practical relevance? Which skills are prerequisites for higher-level capabilities that AI still lacks? What new skills will be essential for working and living effectively with powerful AI systems? Ethical and safety issues Ethical and safety concerns around AI are at the heart of public, media and policy debates. In response to the current generation of deep learning models, issues such as algorithmic discrimination, mass data exploitation and lack of transparency in AI decision making have fueled calls for stronger oversight, ethical safeguards and responsible regulation. 14  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Beyond concerns about the impact of training huge models on the environment and energy infrastructure, most ethical and safety issues related to AI revolve around their capabilities. Scenarios about job automation, for example, often point out that an AI system could make an objectively worse decision than a human. Perhaps it would neglect key factors that a human would consider or be unable to explain a result. In other cases, society may want a person to bear the moral responsibility for a decision – such as deciding to kill an opponent during a war. Society may also believe it is ethically important for a person to carry out a particular task, such as a doctor informing a patient about a fatal illness. Understanding the relevant AI capabilities will be important to appreciating the related ethical and safety issues, including how these concerns may shift as AI capabilities change. The current stage of development of LLMs, for example, has raised great concerns about AI’s hallucinations. Consequently, policymakers should understand the necessity of developing accurate factual recall and human-like critical thinking capabilities to protect us from being misled by AI systems. A quantifiable roadmap to AGI Beyond signaling the risks and opportunities posed by current AI systems, the AI Capability Indicators will also allow policymakers and the public to track AI developments in a systematic and evidenced based way. This will be particularly important as AI systems develop advanced capabilities at or beyond the human level. Tech leaders and commentators have discussed the potential for artificial general intelligence (AGI) and societal risks associated with “singularity” – the moment when AI systems surpass human intelligence across all domains and could potentially result in explosively fast change. When it reaches singularity, could AGI potentially prioritise self-preservation over human interests? Leaders from organisations have divergent opinions on the risks of AGI. Executives at OpenAI (Kelly, 2023[9]) and X (Acres, 2023[10]) have discussed the imminent risk to humanity of AGI. Others at Meta (Collins, 2025[11]), Anthropic (AI Today, 2025[12]) and Google (Dragan et al., 2 April 2025[13]), reference the imminent arrival of AGI without detailing its implications. In 2023, leading researchers and tech CEOs signed an open letter warning that AGI could pose an existential threat to humanity. Should policy makers take these concerns seriously? If not now, then when? The OECD scales provide a timely framework for policy makers to understand the proximity of current systems to AGI and the closer term risks posed by intermediate steps. The scales provide a clear way to characterise an AGI system in human terms: performance at the top of the scale (level 5) indicates full human equivalence. An AI system performing at level 5 could reproduce the full range of human abilities, including all key human aspects of those abilities. Outline of the report The remaining chapters present the beta scales, their development and their potential to be a valuable tool for policy makers to understand AI developments. Chapter 2 by Sam Mitchell, Stuart Elliott and Abel Baret outlines the OECD’s methodology for assessing AI capabilities across human-like skill domains rather than focusing on tasks. It surveys two major information sources – expert opinion and direct AI performance measures – highlighting each one’s strengths and limits. The chapter emphasises that human abilities form a finite set of essential capabilities, which AI is progressively acquiring. It concludes with details on the project’s iterative development process and next steps for refining the indicators. Chapter 3 by Sam Mitchell, Stuart Elliott and Abel Baret discusses the beta AI Capability Indicators’ current shortcomings and outlines steps for their refinement. The chapter highlights potential additions or  15 OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 reorganisations of the scales, clarifies their boundaries and overlap, and emphasises the need to systematically track rapid AI developments. It proposes an ongoing, evidence-based update process, anchored by expert judgement and performance measures. This would be supplemented by a repository for new benchmarks and standards, ensuring the indicators evolve with AI’s progress. Chapter 4 by Yvette Graham, Arthur Graesser and Swen Riberio explore questions around language as one of the OECD Capability Indicators for AI. They consider how many dimensions of difficulty are needed to develop such a scale, reflecting on whether it should focus on the case of communication induced by language or on other aspects, such as reasoning. It also looks at whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems should be defined on a discrete or continuous cale. Finally, it asks whether the main challenge is integration of different language capabilities or improving performance of capabilities like reasoning. After examining the stakes and challenges, it proposes a six-dimensional scale to track advances of NLP and AI. Chapter 5 by António M. Fernandes, Ana Teresa Antunes, Rebecca Ramnauth, Nicholas C. Georgiou, Miguel Faria, Haohua Dong, Regina de Brito Duarte, Joana Brito, Henrique Correia da Fonseca, Ana Vilaça Carrasco, Inês Lobo, Rui Prada, Ana Paiva and Brian Scassellati presents a framework for evaluating the social intelligence of AI agents, structured across five levels and seven social components. Drawing from psychology and human-computer interaction, the chapter identifies core social skills – such as memory, identity and embodiment – and shows how they influence other capabilities. The model helps assess agents like ChatGPT and AIBO, and highlights ethical concerns around trust, influence and inequality linked to socially intelligent agents. Chapter 6 by Kenneth Forbus and Patrick Kyllonen introduces four dimensions for characterising AI problem solving. It presents a five-level scale ranging from domain-specific capabilities to systems with holistic professional expertise. The text emphasises the roles of solution properties, alternatives considered, professional knowledge and model formulation/interpretation. Illustrative benchmarks and examples underscore how current AI excels at well-formalised tasks but struggles with open-ended, socially grounded domains. The chapter concludes by highlighting future research avenues for bridging tacit knowledge and robust reasoning. Chapter 7 by Giorgio Franceschelli and Mirco Musolesi introduces a five-level scale for evaluating AI creativity, built upon four criteria from human creativity research – product, process, press and person. The chapter illustrates how current AI systems often exhibit novelty and value but lack autonomy and intention. It further discusses emerging ethical challenges, the scarcity of comprehensive benchmarks for creative outputs and the societal implications of future AI systems capable of human-like creative agency. Chapter 8 by Christian Lebiere introduces a structured scale for assessing knowledge, learning and memory capabilities in AI systems. By delineating five progressive dimensions – ranging from information retrieval to integrated knowledge – the scale provides a conceptual framework to track and evaluate AI’s cognitive advancements. It also highlights key trade-offs such as accuracy, efficiency and generalisation capacity. Additionally, the chapter introduces a set of measures to evaluate AI models at each level of the scale systematically, comprising computation cost, predictive accuracy, generalisation robustness and incremental learning capabilities. Finally, it touches on ethical considerations related to intellectual property, privacy, bias and manipulation that emerging AI paradigms should address. Chapter 9 by José Hernández-Orallo and Kexin-Jian Chen explore how metacognition and critical thinking have become increasingly relevant with the rise of agentic systems in AI, while remaining difficult to evaluate. The authors developed a scale to present as many domains of human cognition as possible for this study. They propose a five-level scale merging three dimensions: the need for critical thinking processes, the difficulty of calibrating knowns and unknowns, and the difficulty of identifying relevant information. Unlike other capabilities, the rubric can be applied without references to AI or humans and could be annotated using humans or a large language model such as GPT4. 16  OECD AI CAPABILITY INDICATORS TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025 Chapter 10 by Robert B. Fisher, Anthony G. Cohn and Christopher Lochhead assesses the current state of the subdomain of computer vision, comprising the full range of image data: static images, videos, multi-spectral images, microscope, ultrasound and medical scanner image. In addition to a five-level scale comparable to other chapters, it developed a five-level “Sophistication” scale to encapsulate the capability range from highly constrained applications to human level and beyond. It offers three analyses of capabilities using the Sophistication scale and then compares the approaches. A discussion of ethical issues arising from use of the scale follows with a focus on development and deployment issues. The final section reflects on three key limitations to the study related to speed, adversaries and explainability. Chapter 11 by Elena Messina presents a five-level scale for evaluating robotic manipulation – from simple pick-and-place operations under controlled conditions to human-level dexterity. It describes how AI-powered hardware and software, including sensing and planning systems, enable progressively more adaptable, flexible and robust manipulation capabilities. The chapter also surveys current benchmarks and competitions, noting they are fragmented and primarily address lower-level skills. It concludes that current robotic manipulation capabilities are broadly at level 2, with ample scope for further development. Chapter 12 by Jean Oh, Cherie Ho, Rebecca Martin and Jonathan Francis proposes a five-level scale for evaluating robotic intelligence, emphasising how robots must combine multiple AI components – including perception, language, planning and ethics – to operate effectively in real-world environments. The chapter details different task complexities, environmental conditions and interaction requirements that define each level. It concludes with recommendations for multi-level benchmarks, offering both a current capability snapshot and a roadmap towards higher-level, fully autonomous robot intelligence. Chapter 13 by Margarita Kalamova and Gianluca Risi introduces a multi-layered framework for analysing how AI capabilities interact with occupations, tasks and education. Centred on the OECD AI Capability Indicators, the chapter outlines methodologies to map AI’s technical progress onto human ability requirements. It proposes both occupation-level and task-level analyses, drawing on O*NET data to align AI functions with detailed descriptors of language, problem solving, perception, social interaction and manipulation. A key innovation is the development of a Catch-Up Index, a quantitative measure of the gap between current AI capabilities and the demands of jobs or tasks, which enables fine-grained analyses of job and educational transformation as a result of AI. Chapter 14 by Ryota Kanai leverages insights from scientific theories of consciousness to develop a five-level scale. Drawing on the author’s own Information Generation Hypothesis, the chapter elaborates on how the hypothesis provides empirically testable functional criteria relevant to AI systems. It explores the evolutionary stages of mind and consciousness, and how the scale can be applied to evaluate existing AI systems. The chapter concludes by reiterating the limitations of the approach, which should be considered exploratory, provisional and reflective of the author's personal stance rather than as a definitive or universally accepted measure. Included as an annex in this chapter are three reviews of the chapter, deanonymised and published with the permission of the authors. # AI Voice Agents in 2025: Smarter, Faster, but Still Not Human

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=96&d=mm&r=g)

**Eugene Datura**
Content Specialist

![](https://d3upe020n1uosc.cloudfront.net/static/web/images/blog/sidebar/sidebar_banner_chatbots_across_customer_channels.png)

In 2025, AI voice agents are more than a tech trend. According to Juniper Research, over 8.4 billion voice-enabled devices are now active globally. That is more than the population of the planet. The global market is projected to exceed $38 billion by 2026. Companies are integrating voice interfaces into hospitals, banks, retail apps, and education platforms.

These systems now book appointments, give financial updates, and help customers shop hands-free. But do they actually improve service or just replace it with automation? The answers are more nuanced than you might expect.

Below is a practical guide to how voice agents work, where they are useful, what problems they face, and how to get started.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/1-2.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/1-2.png)

## What Is a Conversational AI Voice Agent and Why It Matters

A conversational AI voice agent is a program that listens, understands, and responds like a person. It uses speech recognition to hear what you say, natural language processing to understand the meaning, and machine learning to improve over time.

These agents are changing industries where round-the-clock support and speed are essential. In healthcare, they help patients with appointment scheduling and medication reminders. In customer service, they handle routine questions quickly and consistently. Their ability to work without breaks makes them attractive to organizations facing labor shortages.

In the US, the healthcare sector is expected to face a shortage of over 3.2 million workers by 2026, according to the Association of American Medical Colleges. AI agents can help fill these gaps by handling non-urgent interactions.

You can experiment with this kind of technology using the [Graphlogic Text‑to‑Speech API](https://graphlogic.ai/gl-text-to-speech/), which delivers natural-sounding speech suitable for healthcare, finance, or retail use cases.

## How Voice AI Works: Core Technologies Behind the System

Understanding what is under the hood of voice AI systems is key to using them effectively. Each conversation involves several layers of processing that happen in milliseconds.

Systems that combine all of these layers reliably are often built using platforms like the [Graphlogic Voice Box API](https://docs.graphlogic.ai/voice-box-api-245), which lets developers test and refine AI behavior for their audience.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/2-3.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/2-3.png)

## Which Type of Voice Agent Fits Your Use Case

Not every voice system works the same way. Choosing the right type depends on what kind of problem you want to solve.

If your goal is customer-facing automation with some intelligence, start with an AI agent. If your need is internal productivity, consider deploying a copilot-style integration.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/3-1-1024x682.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/3-1-1024x682.png)

## What You Actually Gain from Voice AI

Many companies turn to voice AI because it cuts costs. But its real value goes beyond that. In successful deployments, the technology improves workflow, reduces user frustration, and adds speed to basic interactions.

These results are only possible when the system is trained well and designed around the actual needs of the users.

## Where Voice Agents Actually Work in 2025

Voice AI has moved beyond tech demos. It is now used in major sectors with real-world outcomes.

In healthcare, systems manage patient check-ins, follow-up reminders, and pre-visit screening. The Mayo Clinic’s voice-based assistant is a widely cited example, offering basic health advice and helping reduce hotline load.

In banking, voice agents help with account balances, transaction history, and fraud alerts. Bank of America’s AI assistant “Erica” processed over 1.5 billion interactions by early 2025, with adoption still growing.

In e-commerce, smart assistants guide users through products, manage orders, and even recommend based on past behavior. Retailers using voice interfaces see cart values increase by as much as 18%, according to internal case studies from Salesforce.

In education, tools like Duolingo have added spoken comprehension testing and pronunciation scoring, improving retention and engagement.

These sectors succeed with voice AI because they focus on repeatable, time-sensitive tasks that do not require emotional nuance.

## Why Voice AI Still Struggles in Some Areas

No technology is perfect, and voice AI comes with limits. These are especially important in sectors like healthcare and finance where precision matters.

To make sure your implementation succeeds, test systems with real users early. Also ensure your platform provider follows encryption and security protocols.

Even the most advanced platforms will misfire without good training data. That is why tools like the [Graphlogic Generative AI Platform](https://graphlogic.ai/generative-ai/) are useful. They support retrieval-augmented generation and domain-specific fine-tuning for more accurate results.

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/4.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/4.png)

## What the Next Generation of Voice AI Will Look Like

By late 2025, voice AI is evolving beyond basic assistants into a more adaptive and multimodal experience. This shift is driven by user demand for smoother, more human-like interaction, as well as by improvements in model training and deployment tools.

Here are some of the main trends shaping the future of voice AI:

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/5.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/5.png)

### Industry Forecasts for 2026 and Beyond

Looking ahead, several forecasts outline where this market is going:

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/6-2.png)

![](http://graphlogic.ai/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/6-2.png)

The takeaway is simple. Voice AI is not just growing. It is being embedded into critical systems that need accuracy, speed, and reliability.
